site.name: Invincible Mine
overview: Invincible Mine is a documented historic mine northwest of Jamestown that shifted from metal mining to fluorspar production during the early twentieth century.
Colorado and federal geological reports describe its broad fluorite vein, shaft, open cut, tunnel and drift workings, while historic Boulder photographs preserve the mine's surface setting.

timeline.text: A surviving Boulder Historical Society photograph documents the Invincible Mine near Jamestown and its mine building.
Colorado Geological Survey reporting described a fluorite vein about 12 feet wide, an open cut southeast of the shaft house, and ore production through a lower tunnel and drift.
Fluorspar from the Invincible was among the Jamestown-district feed processed at the Valmont mill near Boulder for industrial use.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey Bulletin 18 records that the Invincible had formerly been worked as a metalliferous mine before becoming an intermittent fluorspar producer. The report describes a persistent fluorite-rich vein and separate shaft, open-cut, tunnel and drift development.
Later federal work on the Jamestown fluorspar district retained the Invincible as a named mine and documented it within the district's broader fluorite system.

A USGS/GNIS-derived mapped mine point at approximately 40.124152, -105.393883 is used as the historic mine-level identification anchor. It identifies the named mine locality without claiming that a particular surviving shaft or portal has been field surveyed or is safe to approach.
